body.text: When Pakistan’s then-Foreign Minister Hina Rabbani Khar visited India in July 2011, the Indian media went gaga over her appearance. Her Roberto Cavalli designer sunglasses, pearl necklaces, elegant clothes and, above all, her Hermès Birkin handbag became the subject of endless fascination. She was Pakistan’s youngest foreign minister and its first woman to hold the position, but much of the media coverage seemed more interested in what she carried on her arm than what she brought to the negotiating table.

Fed on a diet of stereotypes dominated by terrorism, religious conservatism, economic breakdown, and political instability, the Indian media was taken aback by the sight of a young, fashionable, and articulate Pakistani woman occupying one of the highest positions in her country’s government.

Khar’s glamorous appearance overshadowed the diplomatic significance of the visit. This was the first attempt to revive dialogue between the two nations after 2008 Mumbai terror attacks. Khar herself expressed displeasure at being portrayed as a fashion icon, observing that a male foreign minister would hardly have attracted similar attention for his suit or accessories.

For years, prime-time news debates and mainstream cinema in India have reinforced deeply entrenched preconceived notions and stereotypes, conditioning audiences to view Pakistan through a narrow prism of perpetual conflict, uniform religious extremism, one-dimensional espionage, and exaggerated claims of imminent economic collapse. From viral headlines claiming the country has been left with barely a week’s supply of wheat, sugar, or rice to Bollywood’s reliance on jingoist movies like “Dhurandhar,” “Uri: The Surgical Strike,” “Gadar 2,” and others, Pakistanis were made to look like people from a different planet.

Ironically, the idiot box, rather than Khar, completely changed the stereotypical image of Pakistan. Although Pakistani dramas were available on YouTube, their popularity in India began gathering momentum around 2012–14, particularly with the success of “Humsafar” and “Zindagi Gulzar Hai.” After that, there was no stopping it.
Today, Pakistani dramas have replaced clichéd saas-bahu (daughter-in-law and mother-in-law) sagas because of their nuanced storytelling and compelling narratives.

Marriage and other relatable issues are the mainstay of Pakistani serials; however, Indian viewers discovered a society far more familiar and nuanced than the one they have been conditioned to imagine. Palatial and plush houses, swanky cars, and designer clothes with a Pakistani ethnic touch brought a new image of Pakistan.

Another departure is the portrayal of Muslim culture. Although India has more than 200 million Muslims, Hindi films and serials have often presented stereotypical images of them. Earlier, there used to be an Inspector Khan or Ali, a friend of the hero, or a street urchin in a skullcap and mesh vest, chewing paan (betel leaves).

Nowadays, political polarization has made the Muslim character a villain, an extremist, or a perpetual outsider in many popular narratives. What has been steadily erased in this process is normalcy — the everyday lives of Muslim families navigating work, aspiration, compromise, and survival, like millions of others. Pakistani serials have brought back this sense of normalcy.

Many people argue that shared culture, language, family structures, customs, and social settings make these stories appealing to Indian audiences. This is correct, but it tells only part of the story. A large section of the Indian population is unfamiliar with many Muslim cultural practices. Many have not seen a nikah (Muslim wedding) ceremony or everyday Urdu words that have disappeared from the vocabulary of Indians.

Lastly, given the popularity of Pakistani serials in India, their makers have largely kept political enmity and contentious issues like Kashmir out of their narratives. Instead, they focus on the everyday concerns of people on the other side of the border, allowing viewers to look beyond the political hostility that dominates relations between the two countries.

Fifteen years ago, the Hina Rabbani Khar episode wowed Indians. Today, Abu Bakar, a fictional character in the drama “Dar-e-Nijaat” has become a household favorite in India because of his emotional depth and humanity. The difference is not necessarily that India has changed, but that audiences are increasingly finding ways to look beyond the stereotypes fed to them.
